newsitem.title: GABON: Gabon summit looks for way out for ailing Mobutu.
newsitem.headline: Gabon summit looks for way out for ailing Mobutu.

text.p: Ailing Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko was in the Gabonese capital Libreville on Thursday for a mini-summit which is looking for a way to end fighting with rebels who threaten his capital Kinshasa.

Hundreds of civilians and fighters from both sides were reported dead after a battle for Kenge, a town 200 km (125 miles) east of the capital. Church and humanitarian sources hoped to establish whether massacres had taken place.

A spokesman in the Gabonese president's office, Vincent Mavungu, said the mini-summit aimed to find a negotiated settlement after a weekend meeting between Mobutu and rebel leader Laurent Kabila which promised new talks within 10 days.
"It is therefore normal that consultations take place at all levels to try and find this solution, that is what explains the presence of a certain number of heads of state," Mavungu told reporters.
A U.N. source said he doubted very much whether there would be another face-to-face meeting between Mobutu and Kabila.
"They (the Central African presidents) will try to get Mobutu to withdraw in a dignified way," the source added.
Gabon's president Omar Bongo indicated that Mobutu's poor health had prevented the veteran president from meeting other heads of state on Wednesday.
"You know his state of health," Bongo said.
Mobutu's hold on power has been almost broken by prostate cancer and Kabila's rebels, who control about three-quarters of mineral-rich Zaire after seven months of fighting.
Weekend talks between the civil war foes, hosted by South Africa's Nelson Mandela, ended inconclusively and South Africa said new talks would be held within 10 days.

The Zaire government said Mobutu would in Libreville meet presidents of Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, Congo, Equatorial Guinea and Gabon. All are old friends of Mobutu, who for more than three decades dominated the sprawling country at the heart of Africa.
Aides insisted he would return home by Friday.

But many Zairians said they did not expect, or want, Mobutu to return, and U.S. officials said they believed his return might be unwise. "If he comes back, it's at great risk," one U.S. official said.
Residents of Kenge, in radio contact with Kinshasa, said the rebels were in control of the town on Wednesday after Mobutu's forces recaptured it briefly on Sunday night.
They said at least 200 civilians, 106 government troops and 15 of Laurent Kabila's rebels were killed, while a total of 125 people were injured.
A Western security source said the radio was under guard by rebels monitoring all communication, meaning that details, particularly of casualties, were treated with caution.
A last stand by Mobutu's frightened troops, with nowhere to run after being driven across the country by the rebels, appals residents of Kinshasa and foreign governments alike.
Waiting across the river in Congo, troops from the United States, former colonial power Belgium, France and Britain will step in to evacuate their nationals if there is trouble.

On the humanitarian front, the number of Rwandan Hutu refugees flown home from rebel-held Zaire passed the 10,000 mark on Wednesday but relief officials said tens of thousands of others were either dead or missing in the forests.
